articles.headline: Saints again on losing end of controversial fumble ruling
articles.description: The Saints walked away from Sunday's loss to the Raiders just as confused about the application of the quarterback fumble rules as they were in Week 1.
articles.body:
NEW ORLEANS -- The Saints have now been on the losing end of two controversial calls regarding quarterback fumbles this season.

The Saints (1-2) walked away from Sunday's game, a 35-27 loss to the Las Vegas Raiders (3-0), just as confused about the application of the call as they were in Week 1.

In Week 1, Saints EDGE rusher Chase Young sacked Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff, whose ensuing fumble was picked up and run back for a touchdown. That call was overturned and ruled an incomplete pass because of a little known rule that says any intentional movement of the quarterback's hand starts a forward pass, even if the ball goes backward.

On Sunday, Saints quarterback Tyler Shough appeared to have begun the throwing process when he was hit in the arm and sacked by Raiders linebacker Malcolm Koonce. The football was knocked out of his hand and recovered by defensive end Maxx Crosby. This time, the call stood as a fumble.

"I thought I threw it. Me personally, I thought my arm was going forward," Shough said. "I'm not exactly sure on the rule. It doesn't really matter to me. I've got to get it out sooner regardless."

As Saints fans rained down boos, the videoboard in the Caesars Superdome zoomed in on Young, who shook his head and mimicked throwing an incomplete pass.

"I thought his intent was he threw it forward," Young said later in the locker room, emphasizing the word intent. "But never mind."

"Intent" was the word referee Alan Eck used in Detroit, citing the quarterback's intent to throw the ball forward.

Mark Butterworth, the NFL's vice president of instant replay, said in a pool report Sunday that the defender's right hand hit the ball and Shough's hand.

"The quarterback clearly lost control of the ball before his hand was coming forward," Butterworth said.

Butterworth was asked about the similarities between the two plays and said: "All we are looking for is the hand coming forward with control to make it an incomplete pass. In the play that happened today, the hand was not coming forward with control of the ball."

Butterworth previously said in a pool report regarding the Detroit play: "If the defender contacts the passer prior to the passer starting his throwing motion, it can be ruled as a backward pass. Because Goff had already started his throwing motion, and then the defender contacted him, it is therefore a forward pass."

Shough's strip/sack was the first of four straight turnovers for the Saints in the fourth quarter, which aided the Raiders in a late comeback. The Saints led 27-16 midway through the third quarter before 19 unanswered Raiders points.

articles.headline: Ravens stun Cowboys in final seconds as Loop gains redemption
articles.description: Lamar Jackson, Tyler Loop and the Ravens delivered one of the most remarkable last-second victories in recent NFL history Sunday, thanks to a late fourth-quarter decision made by the Cowboys.
articles.body:
Lamar Jackson and the Baltimore Ravens delivered one of the most remarkable last-second victories in recent NFL history Sunday, thanks to a late fourth-quarter decision made by the Dallas Cowboys.

In a thrilling 34-31 win in Rio de Janeiro, Jackson was able to set up the winning field goal because the Cowboys chose to send the kickoff into the end zone, which ran no time off the clock. After the touchback gave the ball to the Ravens at their 35-yard line with seven seconds remaining, Jackson completed a 27-yard pass to wide receiver Zay Flowers. Tyler Loop then drilled a 56-yard field goal with no time remaining, redemption for the second-year kicker after his miss in last season's finale ended Baltimore's season.

It marked the latest start to a game-winning drive off of a kickoff since 1978 (including playoffs), according to ESPN Research.

"Honestly, anything less than seven seconds, it would have been really hard to do the play that we did," Ravens coach Jesse Minter said. "We may have even just ran the clock out. But [with] seven seconds left ... they decided to kick a touchback [and] gave us the ball on the 35.

"You practice those moments, and you wait for them to come up, it came up today, and we were ready."

Dallas tied the game at 31 with seven seconds remaining after it got to within two yards of the end zone but had to settle for a Brandon Aubrey 23-yard field goal.

Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer said the decision to go for the touchback on the ensuing kickoff was partially made because Aubrey had two kickoffs that went out of bounds earlier and led to Baltimore drives starting at the 40.

"At the end of the day, we just felt like, "Hey, let's boom it through. Let's put them out there, make them throw the ball short and we'll be fine. Play for overtime,'" Schottenheimer said. "And that's what the plan was."

But Jackson had other plans, producing his first game-winning drive that started with less than one minute remaining in the fourth quarter. He called it a "get-down, timeout" situation, which is a scenario the Ravens had been practicing since training camp but not this past week.

Jackson completed a 27-yard pass -- his second-longest completion of the game -- to Flowers over the middle and called timeout immediately to stop the clock with one second left.

"Zay ran a great route and I just had to deliver the baby," said Jackson, who was 6-of-7 for 72 yards in the fourth quarter. "He caught it, and as soon as he got down, I said, 'Please see me [call a timeout], ref,' and he did."

Schottenheimer said he liked the call on that play from defensive coordinator Christian Parker because they wanted to stay "sticky." The Cowboys were playing with a banged-up secondary with Reddy Steward playing in the slot after injuries to Jalen Thompson. Caelen Carson was in the game at cornerback with Shavon Revel out with an injured knee.

articles.headline: Raiders' Brock Bowers shines in return from knee procedure
articles.description: Brock Bowers showed no rust in his regular-season debut Sunday after undergoing a meniscus procedure, finishing with 10 catches for 116 yards and a TD.
articles.body:
NEW ORLEANS -- A meniscus trim and two weeks of being a bystander did not prevent Brock Bowers from delivering a masterclass performance in his regular-season debut on Sunday afternoon.

The third-year tight end once again issued a reminder of why he is one of the best at his position, catching a team-high 10 passes for 116 yards and a touchdown in the Raiders' 35-27 comeback win over the Saints at the Caesars Superdome.

"It felt good to be back," Bowers said.

Bowers' delayed start to the season was necessary as he dealt with pain in his knee throughout training camp. The specific injury wasn't diagnosed until earlier this month, though, prompting surgery with Dr. Daniel Cooper.

"I thought it was nothing," Bowers said. "I thought it would go away before the start of the season, but I had to get it done and get it right before the long stretch of the season."

He returned to the practice field last Friday and has been a limited participant ever since.

Bowers was absent from the team's final practice before traveling to New Orleans. His absence wasn't a concern, as it was a part of the team's plan to have the All-Pro pass catcher fully ready for their matchup against New Orleans, said coach Klint Kubiak.

"To come off an injury and play the way he did was very impressive, and we needed it," said Kubiak.

Despite the Raiders' defense forcing four turnovers and veteran Kirk Cousins continuing to defy his 38-year-old age by throwing three touchdown passes and helping his team overcome a 27-16 deficit, Bowers was the star of the show.

He began the game by catching three passes for 37 yards on three targets during the team's opening drive, which resulted in a 41-yard field goal attempt from kicker Matt Gay. With 19 seconds left in the second quarter, Bowers maintained his balance and stayed in bounds while making a 15-yard grab near the sideline despite Saints safety Jonas Sanker applying sticky coverage.

"We're a better team when he's on the field. That's for sure," center Tyler Linderbaum said. "[Bowers] does it the right way."

While the Raiders were making their comeback in the fourth, Bowers helped strengthen their lead by catching a 3-yard touchdown pass from Cousins with 6:22 to go in regulation.

Cousins was pleased to see the strong connection between him and Bowers translate from training camp practices to an actual game. Still, Cousins said there's more room to grow.

"I had this with [Minnesota Vikings wide receiver Justin Jefferson], where early on you don't realize how good he was as a player," Cousins said. "And then you play with him longer, and you start to realize, 'Oh, practice didn't really show just how good he is,' and so I think games with Brock will be important for us to continue to build that rapport."

articles.headline: How Josh Allen, Bills overcame five turnovers to go to 3-0
articles.description: Buffalo turned the ball over three times on its first four possessions in the 24-16 win over Chargers.
articles.body:
ORCHARD PARK, N.Y. -- The Buffalo Bills were on fire.

Not in the good way.

"Overall, again, we won, but a lot of smoke detectors going off right now," quarterback Josh Allen said after his offense's five-turnover performance in Sunday's 24-16 comeback win over the Los Angeles Chargers. "We got to clean a lot of stuff up."

"The house was on fire today," coach Joe Brady added. "That's unacceptable."

The Bills scored 24 points in the first half in Week 1 and 27 points in the first half in Week 2, but Allen said it felt like a dream to go into halftime in Week 3 tied 10-10. Running back James Cook III fumbled on the first play from scrimmage, and Allen -- who finished 16 of 26 for 204 yards and no passing touchdowns despite rushing for two -- threw interceptions on two of the next three drives. 

So Brady used his halftime speech to take an unlikely stance.

"I told the team at halftime: 'This is perfect,'" Brady told reporters postgame. "I meant that. I wanted to see how we were going to respond. I wanted to see what it was going to reveal. Were we going to be a team that's just going to point fingers when things aren't going well? How are we going to respond?"

It'd be one thing if the speech worked and the Bills came out and body-slammed the Chargers for the next 30 minutes. But the second half was a lot like the first. Two more turnovers. Six penalties for 43 yards. Allen threw for only 82 yards. This was hardly the MVP-frontrunner version of Allen, who glided through the first two weeks of the season seemingly wearing a cape and a utility belt.

And yet, the Bills responded.

"I think it all comes back to Joe Brady," center Connor McGovern told ESPN. "That's what he preaches: We don't break. No matter whether it was the first [turnover] or the fifth or all the different penalties we got, you look at the sideline and we're all ready to go, saying, 'Hey, just put the ball back down.' Until the final whistle blows, we're going to keep playing."

McGovern called it a "full circle" feeling. In the first two weeks when the Bills' defense was struggling and the offense was thriving, the offense would come onto the field with a nod and say "we got you" to their departing defensive teammates. Sunday, the defense was able to return the gesture.

Defensive performances like this one don't come around often. Since 2010, teams that turn the ball over five or more times in a game have allowed an average of 32.7 points per game. This was only the fourth time in the past two decades where a team turned the ball over five times but still won by allowing 16 points or fewer.

Sure, the Chargers made their share of mistakes, too, headlined by quarterback Justin Herbert's interception just outside the red zone when the Chargers had the chance to take a two-score lead early in the fourth quarter.

But to the Bills, the opportunism and the calm confidence they displayed despite moment after moment breaking the wrong way was an indicator of this team's embrace of B

articles.description: Sunday of Week 3 has seen 13 games played, with Lamar Jackson, Jahmyr Gibbs and Sam Darnold having big stat days.
articles.body:
Week 3 of the 2026 NFL season continued Sunday with 14 games, including nine in the early window, and we'll have the best highlights, touchdowns and moments from all of them.

In the early window, Jaylen Warren had a career outing in the Pittsburgh Steelers' win against AFC North rival Cincinnati Bengals, Jameis Winston stepped in to lead the New York Giants to a victory over the Tennessee Titans and the Washington Commanders slipped by the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks.

Among the highlights from the afternoon slate of four games, the Baltimore Ravens stunned the Dallas Cowboys in Rio de Janeiro on a Tyler Loop 56-yard field goal and the Las Vegas Raiders improved to 3-0 after beating the Saints in New Orleans.

articles.headline: 'Not my concern': Ex-Man City boss Mancini brushes off guilty reports
articles.description: Roberto Mancini brushed off reports that his former club Manchester City have been found guilty by the Premier League of financial breaches allegedly committed during his time in charge of the club.
articles.headlineJa: 「自分には関係ない」元マンC監督のマンチーニ氏、有罪報道を一蹴
articles.descriptionJa: ロベルト・マンチーニ氏は、自身が指揮を執っていた期間に犯したとされる財務違反について、古巣のマンチェスター・シティがプレミアリーグから有罪と認定されたとする報道を一蹴しました。
articles.body:
Roberto Mancini brushed off reports that his former club Manchester City have been found guilty by the Premier League of financial breaches allegedly committed during his time as manager.

A source confirmed to ESPN on Friday that City were expected to be found guilty on the vast majority of 115 charges of financial breaches in their legal case with the Premier League.

- Man City verdict will leave a stain and stench on a Premier League era

- Man City vs. Premier League: 115 financial charges explained

- Returning Mancini accepts fans' jeers as Italy beaten by Belgium

Among the alleged breaches cited by the Premier League in 2023 were that City had failed to provide "full details of manager remuneration in its relevant contracts with its manager" between 2009 and 2013, the period in which Mancini was in charge and delivered City's first title in 44 years.

According to German publication Der Spiegel, Mancini is said to have at one point earned £1.45 million in a basic salary and £1.75 million as a consultant for a team controlled by City owner Sheikh Mansour in Abu Dhabi.

But speaking at a news conference in Türkiye on Sunday, the now-Italy coach questioned the reported verdict and said it was a matter for the club, not him.

"It's not an issue that concerns me," he said in Bursa ahead of Monday's UEFA Nations League fixture. "It's nothing new because this matter has been discussed for the last four or five years.

"Manchester City has not been found guilty, and the alleged double contract is not my concern. It's their issue, not mine."

In a statement on Friday, City didn't deny the guilty verdicts and said that the process "remains ongoing."

When contacted by ESPN, the Premier League said it wouldn't comment on a "private and confidential process."

In his own statement on Saturday, Man City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak said "nothing has changed" regarding the case, adding "our confidence and intent in proving the club's innocence is just as strong as when this began."

As well as the 2011-12 Premier League title, Mancini also led Man City to victory in the 2011 FA Cup final during his four seasons at the helm. 

He returned to take charge of Italy for a second time this summer.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.
